In Switzerland, inheritance and gift taxes are not regulated by the Confederation: each canton has full jurisdiction and sets its own rates, deductions and exemptions. In the canton of Schaffhausen, as in all other cantons, the cantonal tax law governs how and when to pay inheritance tax and on any donations received. The closer the relationship, the lower the rate; the further away it is, the greater the tax burden.

## Brief Overview - Maximum deposit of 3 months' rent on a blocked account - Dispute only valid on official cantonal form - Contest rent within 30 days to the conciliation authority
## Key Facts - **What**: Maximum deposit of three months' rent - Base law: Code of Obligations (CO) articles 253 and following - Where: Canton of Schaffhausen (uniform federal laws in Switzerland) - Who: Tenant, landlord, and conciliation authority - Deadline for contestation: 30 days from the initial rent offer - Mandatory document: Official cantonal form for dispute - Blocked account: Held in the tenant's name, separate from the landlord's accounts
The law of rental property in Switzerland, including the Canton of Schaffhausen, is governed by the Code of Obligations (CO) articles 253 and following. These federal laws define uniform rights and obligations for tenants and landlords across all Swiss cantons, ensuring stable legal protection regardless of region.
One of the key provisions concerns the deposit, also known as the guarantee deposit: the landlord can retain a maximum amount equal to three months' rent as a guarantee. This deposit must be made in a blocked account held in the tenant's name, ensuring that the amount remains available to the tenant and cannot be confused with the landlord's accounts or used for other purposes.
The termination of the rental contract by the landlord is only valid if communicated through the official cantonal form. Different forms, verbal communications, informal emails, or unofficial letters have no legal value, even if the landlord believes they have correctly notified the contract. This formal requirement protects the tenant from ambiguous interpretations.
To contest the initial rent proposed by the landlord, the tenant has a 30-day deadline to turn to the conciliation authority for rental disputes in the canton. This procedure is mandatory before resorting to court and is completely free of charge.

### The deposit and the blocked account
The regulation of the deposit is designed to protect the tenant: the money does not remain in the landlord's coffers, but in a separate account that the tenant can control at any time. At the end of the contract, the landlord is obliged to return the deposit within 30 days, deducting only the amounts justified by proven damages or documented arrears.
If the landlord believes that there are rights to compensation (costs for damages to the walls, extraordinary cleaning costs, unmade repairs by the tenant), they must communicate the details of the deductions before retaining part of the deposit. Any arbitrary or unmotivated retention is contestable at the conciliation authority within 30 days. ### How the termination of the contract works in Sciaffusa, Switzerland, and throughout the country, the landlord who intends to terminate the contract must use the official cantonal form. This document contains the mandatory fields (names of the parties, address of the property, precise date of the contract's end) and is available at the cantonal authority for conciliation in matters of rental or can be downloaded from the cantonal administration's website. The termination must be sent in writing, preferably by registered mail with return receipt, in order to have proof of delivery. A verbal communication during a conversation, an informal email, a message, or a letter on personal letterhead has no legal value and does not validly initiate the termination procedure. The legal terms for termination vary depending on the duration of the relationship: - **1 month** during the first year of the contract - 2 months from the second year to the ninth year - 3 months from the tenth year onwards These terms are peremptory: a termination that does not respect the times is null. The landlord cannot terminate the contract at will; they must follow the procedure and the terms prescribed by law. ### Procedure for contesting the initial rent If the tenant believes the initial rent is unjust, excessive compared to the prices in the area, or not in line with the quality and level of the property, they have exactly 30 days to submit an application to the conciliation authority. It is not necessary to resort to a lawyer for this phase: the form can be completed by the tenant themselves. The conciliation authority evaluates whether the proposed rent is congruent with local market prices, the condition of the property, the services provided, and the terms of the contract. If the authority finds grounds for contestation, it can mediate an agreement between the parties or issue a conciliation opinion that, if not appealed, becomes binding. Only after a failed attempt at conciliation can the tenant appeal to the cantonal court, with greater procedural burdens and legal costs. This two-tier system encourages a negotiated and rapid solution. ### The role of the conciliation authority in rental matters The conciliation authority is the neutral cantonal organ that mediates between tenant and landlord in all rental disputes. It receives applications on rent disputes, irregular terminations, unjustified security deposits, disputes over accessory expenses, and other conflicts related to rental. The response times vary by canton, but a complete conciliation procedure typically takes between two and three months. The authority has mediation powers: it can invite both parties to an informal meeting, listen to their reasons, and try to find a reciprocal agreement. If mediation fails, the authority issues a conciliation opinion (binding, subject to subsequent judicial appeal). ## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Checklist for tenant at the time of rental When signing a new rental contract in Sciaffusa, follow these steps to protect your rights:
**1. Check the deposit**: ensure it does not exceed three months' rent and that the landlord provides a written receipt of the amount deposited on a blocked account. Request the bank details of the deposit account. 2. Download the cancellation form: before signing, retrieve the official cancellation form from the Sciaffusa administration website. Keep a copy: you will need it if you have to terminate the contract. 3. Document the condition of the property: at the time of entry, write a written inventory of the rooms (state of walls, floors, fixtures, installations), possibly accompanied by dated photos. This inventory becomes proof of the initial state and protects you from unjustified deductions at the end. 4. Check the rent within 30 days: if the rent seems high compared to other similar rentals in the area (same square footage, location, services), collect comparative data and contact the conciliation authority before the 30-day deadline expires. 5. Keep documentation of everything: keep the original signed contract, payment receipts, any written communications from the landlord. These documents are essential in case of disputes.
### Contacts and resources for Sciaffusa The conciliation authority for rental matters in the Sciaffusa Canton is available at the central cantonal administration. Official forms (cancellation, dispute, appeal) are downloadable from the canton of Sciaffusa's website. The relevant legislation is the Code of Obligations (CO) articles 253-306, available in full on the admin.ch portal (federal legislation). For specific clarifications on federal norms, you can also consult the Federal Office of Justice (OFJ). Some cantons make available informative brochures on rental law downloadable for free from the official website. Check the Sciaffusa portal to see if a local guide is available.
### What to avoid Do not waive the request for a blocked account for the deposit (it is your right). Do not accept verbal or informal cancellation forms: the landlord must use the official cantonal form. Do not delay beyond 30 days if you want to contest the initial rent, as the deadline is non-negotiable and not extendable.
### Next steps If you are currently in a rental dispute (contested rent, non-reimbursed deposit, irregular cancellation), the first step is to contact the conciliation authority of your canton without delay. The service is free and resolves most cases within 2-3 months, avoiding legal fees and lengthy judicial proceedings. ### What is apprenticeship in Switzerland
Apprenticeship is the privileged vocational training path in the Swiss education system. It is based on the dual education model: the apprentice spends part of the week in the company (learning the practical trade) and part in the vocational school (acquiring theoretical and general skills). The standard duration is 3 to 4 years, depending on the chosen profession and the canton where the internship is carried out, including ### Progressive Apprentice Pay
The apprentice's salary is set in the internship contract and increases progressively over the 3-4 years. There is no federal minimum wage in Switzerland, however many cantons, including Schaffhausen, have cantonal guidelines or collective bargaining agreements (CCLs) that define guiding minimum wages for traineeships. Generally, the salary increases with each year of internship (lowest first year, highest last year), reflecting the skills progressively acquired.
The amount of remuneration varies significantly by sector of activity (crafts, trade, industry, health have different ranges), by canton (Schaffhausen has specific guidelines) and by company size and applicability of collective agreements. During the internship, the apprentice is entitled to paid holidays: minimum 5 weeks for those under 20, 4 weeks from 20 years onwards. This is a right guaranteed by the Swiss Federal Labour Law.
### Apprentice rights during the internship
The apprentice has the right to training in accordance with the training plan approved by the canton, protection of health and safety at work guaranteed by LAINF (Federal Law on Accident Insurance), systematic teaching of professional skills by the training company, paid holidays, and payment of social contributions (AVS/AI) by the company.

item.title: Gas, a new option for winter in Switzerland
item.description: The Confederation activates the ITA.SWAPtion.26 option to access the France-Italy gas pipeline. Cost 2-3 francs per family. Available from October 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - New gas option «ITA.SWAPtion.26» available from October to 31 March 2027 - Cost per single-family home: CHF 2-3 - Corresponds to about 10% of Swiss winter consumption
## Key facts - **What**: Access to the France-Italy gas pipeline to draw emergency gas - When: Start of October 2026 - 31 March 2027 - Where: Switzerland (regional gas networks) - Who: Federal Office for Economic Supply (FSO) - Activation cost: A few million francs (divided among customers) - Household impact: 2-3 francs per house with gas heating
Ahead of the coming winter, the Confederation is strengthening its gas supply by activating a new security option. The Swiss Federal Office for Economic Supply (AEP) has announced that Switzerland will be able to draw on the transit gas pipeline from France to Italy if necessary, through the option called ITA.SWAPtion.26.
This measure represents a direct response to low reserve levels in EU Member States and uncertainties in international energy markets. Switzerland, we remember, has no seasonal gas storage of its own and is completely dependent on imports.
### What is the ITA.SWAPtion.26 option
The new option allows the country, if necessary, to use the gas flowing through the France-Italy pipeline for its supply. This solution is particularly relevant ### Differentiated protection for categories of customers
Switzerland has adopted a hierarchical protection mechanism in the event of a serious gas shortage. So-called 'unprotected' customers — mainly industries — would be subject to restrictions before vulnerable categories. "Protected" customers include hospitals, emergency services and families, ensuring continuity of essential service in a scenario of energy crisis.
This hierarchy is particularly relevant for Swiss industrial sectors, where even a temporary supply disruption could have significant economic impacts. Large industrial consumers will face considerably higher additional costs than households and will have lower priority in receiving supplies in case of shortages.
### Trilateral Solidarity Agreement
Switzerland, Germany and Italy have signed a solidarity agreement that will enter into force if circumstances so require. In the event of a serious shortage and once all possible measures have been exhausted at national level, protected customers will be able to continue to receive gas supplies from these two European partners. This mechanism represents an additional safety net in case the ITA.SWAPtion.26 option is not sufficient.
The trilateral agreement highlights how energy security in Europe has become a matter of regional cooperation. No European countries
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Timeline and practical requirements
The ITA.SWAPtion.26 option formally enters into force in early October 2026 and remains active until March 31, 2027. During this timeframe, regional gas network operators, through Axpo and OpenEP, are required to maintain operational access to the France-Italy pipeline and manage activation procedures if requested by federal authorities.
For final consumers, no specific action is required during the «option availability» phase. However, it is advisable to monitor communications from your regional network operators or gas suppliers, who should promptly inform you of any changes in supply methods or price increases.
### Gas bill verification
The registration of additional costs for the activation of the option will take place automatically in the months when the measure is operational, starting from October 2026. For a single-family home, the expected amount is 2-3 francs for the entire period (from October 2026 to March 2027), a marginal figure compared to the total winter heating costs.
It is important to check that an item corresponding to this measure appears on your gas bill, in order to verify that the contribution has actually been charged. If the item is missing, you can contact your supplier or regional network operator directly.
### Contacts and sources of information
Regional gas network operators are the primary sources of information for specific details on the measure. Each region has its own operators, and communication methods and application details may vary slightly from one area to another. The Confederation has entrusted the operational management precisely to these regional entities, ensuring coordinated implementation at the national level.
For those wishing to learn more about federal energy policy and security of supply measures, the Federal Office for National Economic Supply (FONES) represents the institutional reference point.
### Winter preparation and conscious behavior
This measure is part of a broader framework to strengthen national energy resilience ahead of the cold season. The Confederation has clearly indicated that the measure is precautionary: it does not reflect an imminent gas shortage, but aims to prepare the country for potentially critical scenarios on international markets.
Consumers and businesses should consider this window (October 2026-March 2027) as a period during which energy security has been institutionally enhanced. However, good energy efficiency practices — thermal insulation of buildings, heating regulation, conscious behavior — always remain relevant regardless of federal security measures, both from an economic and environmental perspective.

item.title: Ticino hospital planning: adequate 2019 data?
item.description: The PLR question on the consultation started on 1 June 2026 raises doubts about the statistical basis of hospital needs in the canton.
item.content:encoded:
## In Brief - Consultation launched on June 1, 2026 on hospital mandates - Questioning on data from 2019 used for calculation of need - Risk of overestimation of need and impact on healthcare costs
## Key Facts - **What**: Inquiry on hospital planning and calculation of need - When: Consultation started on June 1, 2026 - Where: Ticino - Who: Matteo Quadranti (PLR group leader) at the State Council - Sectors: Acute care, rehabilitation, psychiatry - Data base: Data from 2019 (chosen by the commission in 2022)
The Ticino State Council launched a consultation on June 1, 2026 on the proposal for the attribution of hospital performance mandates in the acute care, rehabilitation, and psychiatry sectors. An inquiry by Matteo Quadranti, PLR group leader, questions the technical criteria used to determine the need underlying this planning.
At the center of the issue is the choice to rely on data from 2019 to estimate the need. When the consultative commission was established in 2022, these represented the most recent available: data from 2020 and 2021 had been compromised by the pandemic. Today, however, according to prio.swiss (one of the consulted organizations), this statistical base may not adequately reflect the current reality of the Ticino healthcare system.
Quadranti submits the State Council with a series of specific questions. Firstly, he asks to identify the criticisms emerged during the consultation procedure among the other actors of the healthcare system. Secondly, he raises the risk that a calculation of the need based on data now seven years old (at the time of the publication of the planning in 2026) may lead to an overestimation of the stationary offer necessary.
### The role of reforms in the healthcare sector
The PLR highlights a procedural aspect of relevance: the non-consideration of the normative and organizational evolutions of the last years, in particular the push towards the ambulatory and the implementation of the EFAS. If these changes are not incorporated into the calculation, the risk is of attributing a number of mandates higher than the effective need, with repercussions on healthcare costs.
The consultation remains open to the observations of the stakeholders. Quadranti finally poses a crucial procedural question: a planning built on potentially erroneous statistical bases may expose the Government to appeals, thus blocking its implementation for the next years and creating uncertainty for the Ticino healthcare sector. The response of the State Council to this inquiry will therefore be decisive in clarifying the trajectory of the cantonal hospital planning and its impact on the [LAMal](nav:health) for residents. ### Because outdated data weighs on planning
The question raised by Quadranti touches on a fundamental technical aspect of health planning: the quality and topicality of the statistical base. Using data from seven years earlier (2019 for a plan published in 2026) implies assuming that demand and supply of hospital services remain constant, which is rarely true in reality.
Between 2019 and 2026, the Ticino and national health system underwent significant transformations. In the period considered, EFAs was implemented and the push towards outpatient care accelerated, potentially reducing the demand for traditional beds. If the calculation of the requirement does not complement these developments, it is likely to overestimate the necessary supply.
Overestimating needs has direct consequences on costs. If too many mandates are assigned (hospital performance contracts), the offer expands beyond what is necessary. The costs remain the responsibility of [LAMal](nav:health), the mandatory health insurance for Swiss residents. Greater supply does not necessarily mean better care: it often incentivises non-essential performance, with an impact on the [costo della vita](nav:cost-of-living) for Swiss families.

## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### What post-pandemic data is available? One of the central questions posed by Quadranti concerns the availability of more recent data for a potential update of the hospital demand calculation. When the Government responds, it will be possible to evaluate whether a planning based on 2023, 2024, or 2025 data would be feasible from an administrative point of view. The availability of complete statistical data — clinical outcomes, number of hospitalizations, average length of stay, diagnoses — depends on the information systems of the cantons and the reporting obligations to the Confederation. Typically, these data have a 12-18 month lag compared to the reference period: 2024 data may be complete only in 2025-2026. It is therefore possible that, at the time of the summer consultation in 2026, the most recent available data would still be those of 2024 or 2023, and not yet those of 2025. ### What changes if the calculation is updated If the Government decides to update the hospital demand calculation based on post-pandemic data, the planning may be revised according to three scenarios: **Minimum scenario**: demand is lower than that calculated with 2019 data. Ambulatory care predominance reduces stationary demand. Reduced mandates, lower overall costs for LAMal. Medium scenario: demand remains similar to that calculated. Planning remains substantially unchanged compared to the initial proposal. Maximum scenario: demand is higher than estimated. Unforeseen clinical needs, increased population or clinical complexity. Increased mandates, potentially higher costs. Quadranti explicitly asks the Government where the most recent post-pandemic data sit in relation to these three scenarios, in order to evaluate whether the current planning reflects reality. ### Next steps and impact on the healthcare system The response of the State Council to this interrogation will be public and will contribute to defining the trajectory of Ticinese hospital planning. If the Government decides to update the calculation, this would involve a revision of the consultation and the implementation schedule. If, instead, it maintains the 2019 base, it will need to justify this choice and manage the risk of legal challenges. Swiss residents, particularly those in Ticino, have a direct interest in a solid and transparent hospital planning, as it affects the overall efficiency of LAMal and the premiums they pay to the sick funds. Greater clarity on the technical basis of the planning is therefore in the interest of all insured parties.

item.title: Federal Council adopts 2027 budget
item.description: On August 19, the Federal Council approves the 2027 budget with PICF 2028-2030. Document available online at aff.admin.ch.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Federal Council adopts on August 19, 2026 the federal budget 2027 - Document available online immediately, paper version at the beginning of September - Includes PICF 2028–2030 for four-year planning of the Confederation
## Key facts - **What**: Quote 2027 with integrated plan of tasks and finances 2028–2030 - When: 19 August 2026 (adoption), 20 August 2026 (press release) - Where: Federal Administration of Finance (AFF), aff.admin.ch website - Who: Federal Council and Federal Assembly - Structure: 2 volumes + interactive data portal
The Federal Council formally adopted on 19 August 2026 the message concerning the Swiss Confederation's budget for 2027, accompanied by the integrated plan of tasks and finances (PICF) for the three-year period 2028–2030. The Executive thus makes available the overall document that contains all the income and expenditure of the Confederation planned for next year, in addition to the financial forecasts for the following three years of planning.
The press release published on 20 August 2026 follows the announcement of the benchmarks for 2027 communicated on 24 June 2026. The quote is already available in electronic form on the website of the Federal Administration of Finance (AFF). The paper version will be published at the beginning of September.
### Structure and content of the federal message
The message regarding the 2027 quote with PICF is ### What is PICF and how does it work
The PICF (Integrated Task and Finance Plan) is the multiannual financial planning tool of the Swiss Confederation. Each year, the Federal Council submits to the Federal Assembly a message containing the estimate for the current year accompanied by the PICF for the following three years. This multi-year approach allows expenditure and investment planning to be aligned with federal and cantonal strategic objectives over a broad timeframe.
The PICF reports, for each year of the planning (2027–2030 in the case of the new document), the estimates of revenues and investment income, as well as the totality of the expenditure and estimated income of the Confederation. This means that the document represents not only a final budget, but a forward planning that guides the decisions of the Federal Administration and provides Parliament with a clear vision of the spending priorities for the four years concerned.
### What the quote shows for each federal office
A crucial aspect of the PICF is the breakdown by individual administrative unit. For each federal department and office, the document outlines the task plan, performance groups, and main objectives for the planning period. This allows citizens, media, researchers and economic operators to understand how the Confederation allocates resources
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### How to view the 2027 budget online
The 2027 budget with PICF is already accessible electronically via the Federal Finance Administration website (aff.admin.ch). Citizens do not have to wait for the publication of the paper version scheduled for early September to consult the document: simply visit the FFA portal and access the section dedicated to federal budget documents.
Several consultation methods are available on the website: the complete message in a downloadable PDF format; the overview of federal finances with summary charts; the interactive data portal with graphical representations of financial flows. The data portal is particularly useful for those who wish to analyze in detail how the Confederation plans revenues and expenditures for the 2027-2030 period.
### Next steps: from adoption to the Federal Assembly
Following the Federal Council's approval on August 19, 2026, the budget will be submitted to the Federal Assembly for debate and a vote. The competent parliamentary committees (Finance Committees of the House and Senate) will analyze the document in detail before the plenary debate. Any changes proposed by deputies and senators may impact the final destination of federal funds for 2027 and subsequent years.
For those who live and work in Switzerland, the budget represents a document of transparency: it allows you to verify how the Confederation estimates its revenues (mainly from direct federal taxes and VAT) and how it intends to allocate resources across the various areas of federal competence (healthcare, social security, defense, environment, economy). Zurich — The Swiss insurance sector closed 2025 in a state of robust financial soundness. This assessment was released today by the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA) through its annual report dedicated to the sector. Swiss insurance companies recorded an aggregate annual result of 24.4 billion francs in 2025, representing a dramatic 136% increase compared to the 14 billion francs registered in 2024.
Growth is not uniform across the various insurance branches. Non-life insurers achieved profits of 12.9 billion francs, while reinsurers reached 9.8 billion francs. Life insurers, although growing, posted a more modest increase: their aggregate annual result rose by 10.2% to reach 1.7 billion francs.
### Investments as a growth driver
FINMA highlights how investments represented one of the decisive factors in the positive results. 📊 Investment earnings in the sector increased by 47.6%, settling at 24.8 billion francs. The average return on insurance investments rose to 5.00%, a significant performance when compared to 3.37% the previous year.
### Gross premium trends
On the gross premiums side, the picture is slightly different. Total volume decreased by 0.6%, stopping at 149 billion francs. However, trends vary considerably by branch: life insurers recorded a 3.7% increase in gross premiums, while property and casualty insurers posted a 2.8% increase. Reinsurers, conversely, suffered a 6.1% drop, mainly due to the appreciation of the Swiss franc against the US dollar, the euro, and the British pound. Every year you have the right to change health insurance funds, usually by giving notice by November 30 for effectiveness on December 31. Although the sector is solid — as certified by FINMA 2025 data — this does not mean that all insurers offer the same conditions. Premiums vary significantly by canton and age group, and health insurance funds often offer different deductibles (300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000, or 2500 francs for adults).

Each canton recognizes subsidies (premium reductions) for residents with income below certain thresholds. These subsidies are financed by the cantons themselves and vary considerably: some cantons offer reductions of up to 60-80% of the premium, others less. Inquire with the competent office in your canton (usually the Social Insurance Office or the Health Section) to find out if you are eligible.

LAMal covers basic healthcare costs, but there are risks not covered, such as dental treatments, intensive physiotherapy, or stays in private clinics. Compare offers from the same health insurance funds or specialized companies.

Do not wait for the turn of the year to review your contract. Whenever your situation changes (new job, marriage, birth, moving to another canton), review your coverage. item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - 95 unleaded petrol: 2.02 CHF/litre, first pass since 2022 - Diesel at 2.27 CHF/litre; both +0.05 CHF in a week - Causes: Middle East conflicts, Rhine logistics, refining capacity
## Key facts - **What**: Historical gasoline price threshold exceeded - When: August 2026 (first time since 2022) - Where: Switzerland, national average - Who: TCS (Swiss Touring Club) - Petrol: 2.02 CHF/litre (+0.05 CHF weekly) - Diesel: CHF 2.27/litre (+0.05 CHF weekly) - Comparison 2022: CHF 2.31 (petrol) and CHF 2.40 (diesel)
The Swiss Touring Club (TCS) has announced an alarming new figure on the fuel front. The average price of unleaded petrol 95 has exceeded the critical threshold of 2 francs per litre for the first time since 2022. Specifically, the cost stands at 2.02 francs per litre on a national basis, with an increase of 5 cents recorded in just seven days.
Diesel advances at the same pace, reaching 2.27 francs per litre. Here too, the weekly increase is 5 cents. The announcement comes in a context of global energy price rises, with direct repercussions on the spending of Swiss households.
## # What drives prices up
The TCS has identified multiple causes behind the increase. Geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and reduced global refining capacities are the primary factors. To these are added the damage suffered by several ### The comparison with the 2022 peak
Although the increase is evident, it's useful to place the data in a historical context. In 2022, during the energy crisis following the war in Ukraine, unleaded gasoline 95 reached prices of up to 2.31 francs per liter, while diesel prices approached 2.40 francs. The current prices remain below the four-year highs, but the trend is clearly rising.
### The perfect logistical storm
What makes the situation particularly critical is the convergence of several unfavorable factors. It's not just a simple geopolitical tension — although that is serious — but a combination of phenomena that reinforce each other. The reduction in refining capacity has narrowed the global supply. Conflicts have added uncertainty to investments and directly hit some strategic facilities.
The Rhine drought, caused by adverse climate conditions, has crippled one of Europe's main logistical arteries for fuel transportation to Switzerland. Tanker ships cannot fully load due to insufficient depth. This means that less fuel passes from Rotterdam to Basel, creating a bottleneck that directly affects Swiss prices.
### Short-term prospects
The TCS does not offer reassuring prospects. The institute notes that in the short term, in light of the persistence of the geopolitical situation, the limited refining capacity, and the ongoing transportation problems, it is not reasonable to expect a significant drop in prices. Those who drive daily or rely on merchandise transportation will have to adapt to a structurally more expensive context in the medium term.
For those managing corporate fleets or operating in merchandise transportation, this represents an additional pressure on margins. [Logistics costs directly affect the final cost of consumer goods](nav:cost-of-living), with potential diffused inflationary reflections in the national economy.

It's not a huge amount in itself, but the data is significant if multiplied by millions of car users and fleet managers.
Logistical costs for companies will inevitably increase. Prices for goods transported by road will face upward pressure. The public transportation and services sector will need to assess whether to pass on some of the costs to ticket and tariff prices.

This slowdown reflects a year characterized by less immigration and more emigration, confirming the trends observed in the provisional data released in April 2026.
The profile of the population is transformed. Among the 9,127 million inhabitants, 6,599,000 have Swiss nationality (72%), while 2,528,100 are foreigners (28%). In 2025, the Swiss population grew by 27,900 people (+0.4%), while the foreign population increased by 48,200 people (+1.9%). ### Internal mobility on the decline Alongside comprehensive demographic data, the UST has provided information on population mobility within the Swiss territory. In 2025, 511,200 internal migrations were recorded: 358,000 intracantonal (within the same canton) and 153,200 intercantonal (between different cantons). When related to the number of inhabitants, these numbers highlight a trend of slowdown: only 56 movements per 1,000 inhabitants in 2025, compared to 61 per 1,000 inhabitants ten years earlier. This decline in internal mobility affects both nationality groups, albeit in different ways. In 2025, foreign people maintain a higher mobility compared to Swiss citizens (80 movements per 1,000 foreigners, against 47 per 1,000 Swiss citizens). However, it is precisely among Swiss citizens that the decline in mobility is more marked from 2021 onwards, suggesting growing residential stability or possible economic constraints related to housing costs. ### Pension system under pressure The UST's demographic data has direct repercussions on the sustainability of the Swiss pension system. When the elderly surpass the young, the ratio between active contributors and pensioners narrows, exerting financial pressure on AVS (Old Age Insurance) and LPP (Professional Pension). The natural population growth (only 8% of total growth in 2025) suggests that Switzerland will still rely on migratory balance for many years to maintain an adequate number of active workers. However, the decline in migratory balance in 2025 (-14.9%) indicates that this source of supply is weakening. At the territorial level, the 17 cantons with an older population will face more consistent welfare, health, and long-term care needs, while the nine cantons with younger demographic profiles can count on a broader contributory base. Consult our tools to verify your pension position. The variability between cantons suggests that demographic pressures are not uniform: Vaud, Geneva, Fribourg, and Zurich still maintain younger profiles, while other regions will face more acute sustainability challenges. ### Nationality and labor market dynamics The decline in immigration (-3.9% compared to 2024) and the increase in emigration (+3.1%) indicate changes in the attractive forces of the Swiss labor market. Among new immigrants, Germans remain the largest group (12.9% of flows), followed by Swiss returnees (11.3%), French (10.1%), and Italians (9.1%). On the other hand, Swiss emigration (22% of those leaving the country) suggests a search for opportunities abroad, while that of Portuguese, Italians, and French may reflect economic changes in their countries of origin. These migratory flows have direct effects on the Swiss labor market: fewer immigrants mean less labor supply for certain sectors (construction, hospitality, healthcare), but also less pressure on Swiss citizens' salaries, at least in the short term. [Check the cost of living and job opportunities in your region](nav:cost-of-living) to evaluate your position.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Planning for retirement in a context of aging The demographic implications presented by the UST data have a direct relevance for those planning their own retirement. With a growing life expectancy and an increasingly unfavorable ratio between active and pensioners, it is essential not to rely solely on the AVS guarantee. The contribution rates for the second pillar (LPP) vary by age group: from 7% between 25 and 34 years, to 10% between 35 and 44 years, to 15% between 45 and 54 years, up to 18% after 55 years up to the reference age. This means that the last years of career require a significantly higher contribution effort.
Anyone in one of the higher age groups should check if their LPP rate is correct and if the accumulated capital is sufficient. It is equally important to evaluate the opening of a third pillar account (3a) to integrate the obligatory pension. These tools allow for federal and cantonal tax deductions, reducing the tax burden while accumulating additional capital for retirement.
### Cost of living and housing dynamics The slowdown in demographic growth does not necessarily mean a decline in the cost of living in Switzerland. Rather, aging of the population implies a reconfiguration of housing demand: fewer expanding family units, more pensioners seeking housing solutions tailored to their needs. This phenomenon is reflected in property prices and rents at the local level, with marked variations between cantons. The cantons with the youngest population (Vaud, Geneva, Fribourg, Zurich) are likely to continue exerting pressure on prices, while those with more elderly populations may see emerging housing opportunities at a lower price.
For those living and working in Switzerland, monitoring local cost of living, LAMal premiums (obligatory health insurance), and cantonal taxes remains essential. The older cantons may be pushed to increase taxes to finance welfare, while the younger ones may be able to maintain a more competitive tax system.
### Labor mobility and contractual opportunities The observed decline in internal mobility (56 moves per 1,000 inhabitants in 2025, compared to 61 ten years ago) suggests that workers remain more stable in their places of residence. This trend may reflect a greater difficulty in finding accessible housing in other regions, or a greater preference for telework and flexibility. For employers, it means that the local pool of competitive talent is reduced, prompting them to invest more in internal training and job attractiveness.
Those looking for work in Switzerland should take advantage of this trend: the relative scarcity of mobile candidates amplifies personal bargaining power. It is advisable to negotiate flexibility in working hours, telework, performance bonuses, and salary supplements. Similarly, those already employed may find more favorable conditions in a job change, thanks to the sustained demand for talent in a context of general reduced mobility.

This means that you generally need to have an employment contract or a promise of employment from an employer located in the canton (or Switzerland in general). The Swiss labour market is based on uniform federal protection and cantonal integrations that allow the cantons to define some specific standards. In the canton of Basel-Country, as in the other cantons, the federal regulatory framework (working hours, holiday rights, unemployment protection) coexists with cantonal rules on taxation, supplementary pension and minimum wage where provided.
### Working hours and basic rights
Switzerland sets a maximum time of 45 hours per week for industry, offices and sales, while in other sectors (agriculture, construction) the maximum is 50 hours. These federal limits apply uniformly throughout the territory. ### Taxation and social contributions on salary
Each Swiss salary is withheld for three main categories of contributions and taxes:
1. ** Compulsory social contributions ** (federal): AVS (old-age pension) and AI (disability) together represent 5.3% borne by the employee; the employer pays an additional 5.3% (total 10.6%). The same item includes the IPG (Compensation for loss of earnings, which covers maternity and paternity). Unemployment insurance (AD/AC): 1.1% up to an annual ceiling.
2. Accident insurance (LAINF/LAA): from 0.7% to 1.5% depending on the sector, often paid in full by the employer.
3. LPP — Occupational pension (second pillar): at least 7% of the coordinated salary from 25 to 34 years, up to 18% from 55 years. The LPP is mandatory in Switzerland starting from CHF 21'330 of annual salary (indexed data every year). An important exception: freelancers and freelancers do not have a federal LPP obligation, but can join voluntarily.
4. Direct federal, cantonal and municipal tax: An employee in Switzerland pays three levels of income tax. The federal tax uses uniform progressive rates throughout Switzerland. Each canton sets its own rates and tables (Basel Country has its own tables). The municipality applies a multiplier to the cantonal tax base, creating variability at the local level as well. The combination of these three levels determines the overall effective tax rate.

If your sector has a specific CCL, the working hours may be lower (e.g., 42-43 hours). Always ask for a copy of the applicable CCL for your role.
2. Gross Salary: Clearly ask if the proposed amount is gross or already net. In Switzerland, the salary indicated in a job offer is always gross. The net amount you will receive will be reduced for AVS/AI contributions (5.3%), unemployment (1.1%), LPP (7-18% depending on age and coordinated salary), federal, cantonal, and communal taxes, and LAMal (separate payment).
3. Sickness Fund: Ask if the company has agreements with specific funds or if there is a free choice. Remember that you must conclude the LAMal within 3 months of hiring; the 2026 premiums for Basilea Campagna must be requested directly from the funds (the company does not pay them, unless there are additional company agreements).
4. Old-Age Provision (LPP): If the salary exceeds CHF 21,330 per year, LPP is mandatory. The company has a collective LPP fund; you will receive a fund regulation and a forecast of the accumulated capital at the age of retirement. Read the essential points: contribution rates by age range, guaranteed interest rates, management fees.
5. Termination: The contract must specify the probation period (if any) and the terms of termination thereafter. Federal law: 1 month in the first year, 2 months from the second to the ninth year, 3 months from the tenth year onwards. Some CCLs allow 1 month always.
6. Holidays and Leave: Minimum 4 weeks by federal law. Some CCLs guarantee 5 or 6 weeks. Ask if they are scheduled or at your discretion.

item.title: Apprenticeship in Switzerland: contracts, salary and maturity
item.description: Internship contracts, remuneration, compulsory contributions and professional maturity: an apprenticeship guide in the Swiss training system.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Apprenticeship lasts 3-4 years and combines practical work and school education - AVS/AI contributions: 5.3% for the apprentice (10.6% for employer) - Minimum holidays: 4 weeks (5 under 20 years old) - Federal contract: the same rights in every Swiss canton
## Key facts - **What**: Dual education system that alternates practical work and vocational school - Where: All Swiss cantons, including Basel-Landschaft - Who: Young people from 15 years old and up - Duration: 3-4 years depending on the professional field - Mandatory contributions: AVS/AI 5.3% (employee), 10.6% (employer) - Maximum hours: 45 hours/week (industry, offices, sales) or 50 in other sectors
Apprenticeship is the heart of the Swiss vocational education system. It represents a path combining education and work: the student spends approximately 3-4 days a week in the company and one-two days in vocational school. In the canton of Basel-Landschaft, as in other cantons, the system follows uniform federal rules that define rights, duties and protections for anyone undertaking this path.
The apprenticeship contract is the fundamental document. Regulated by federal law, it must contain the company's data, the apprentice's details, the professional sector, the start date, the total duration, the weekly hours and the remuneration. Once signed by the company and apprentice (with parents or whoever exercises parental authority, if a minor), the contract acquires legal validity.
Working hours must not exceed 45 hours per week in industry, offices and sales, or 50 hours in other sectors. The apprentice is entitled to a minimum of 4 weeks of annual holidays — 5 weeks if under 20. These protections are guaranteed by federal law and apply uniformly in all cantons.
### How the remuneration system works
The apprentice's remuneration is established in the apprenticeship contract. There is no federal minimum wage, although many cantons have defined regional ones and several sectors have collective agreements. During the salary, the apprentice automatically pays 5.3% of AVS/AI contributions (the employer adds 10.6% to their account). Additionally, 1.1% up to the annual limit goes to unemployment insurance (UIC/UCA).
Accident insurance (LAINF/LAI) ranges between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector of activity and is covered by the employer. The LPP pension system (second pillar) usually does not apply to apprentices, as the remuneration is often below the coordination threshold. With the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) online it is possible to estimate net and charges on a hypothetical remuneration. ### Rights and protections during training
The traineeship contract must be filed with the competent cantonal office — in the canton of Basel-Country with the Vocational Training Office. The apprentice always receives a signed copy of the contract. If during the probationary period (usually 1-3 months) incompatibilities arise between the young person and the employer, the contract may be terminated with 1 week's notice by both parties.
After the probationary period, cancellation times are tightened: 1 month in the first year of apprenticeship, 2 months from the second to the ninth year, 3 months from the tenth year onwards. These times are established by federal law and apply in each canton.
Social contributions represent an important voice for those who hire an apprentice. On the one hand, the young person sees 5.3% of AVS/AI and 1.1% of AD/AC deducted from his net; on the other, the employer pays 10.6% of AVS/AI, 1.1% of AD/AC and the cost of LAINF/LAA accident insurance (0.7%-1.5% depending on the sector). All these payments are mandatory by federal law and identical in each canton.
### Health insurance and taxes
Health insurance (LAMal/KVG) is mandatory for anyone residing in Switzerland. The apprentice must stipulate it within 3 months of the start of the training. Premiums are determined by canton and tariff region; the canton Basel-Country has its own tariffs. Adult deductibles range from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500 depending on plan
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Professional Maturity: Additional Qualification
Professional maturity is an additional qualification that apprentices can obtain in parallel with their apprenticeship or immediately after its conclusion. It consists of theoretical lessons in general subjects — languages, mathematics, history, economics, sciences — along with the practical training in the company. At the end of the apprenticeship, the young person obtains both the certificate of competence (AFC, federal apprenticeship diploma) and, if they have attended the mandatory courses, the professional maturity certificate.
Professional maturity is recognized at the federal level and is a privileged gateway to access professional university schools (SUP). Many cantons, including Basel-Landschaft, offer maturity courses at ordinary professional schools. The cost is usually free or minimal for the apprentice; the school is financed by the canton itself. Completing professional maturity simultaneously with the apprenticeship requires organization, but allows for further qualification without extending the overall training time.
### How to Find and Start an Apprenticeship
Searching for an apprenticeship position takes place mainly through national and regional job advertisement portals, the local employment office, direct contacts with companies in the field of interest, and school orientation fairs. Once a potential employer is found, the negotiation of the apprenticeship contract proceeds.
Before signing, it is essential to verify that the document contains: the name and address of the company, the name and date of birth of the apprentice, the professional branch, start date, total duration in years, declared weekly hours, monthly or annual remuneration and payment methods. The cantonal professional education office of Basel-Landschaft can provide advice on contractual standards and minimum rights.
### Next Steps
To navigate the world of apprenticeships and estimate your net salary after contributions and taxes, use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator). To search for apprenticeship offers in the canton of Basel-Landschaft, access specialized [job board](nav:jobs) portals, which allow you to filter by region, sector, and type of training. If you have questions about contracts, rights, hours, or contributions during the apprenticeship, the cantonal professional education office remains the main reference.

Those who move to Switzerland from abroad and have a valid driving license in their country of origin cannot drive indefinitely with the foreign document. The Federal Road Traffic Act requires foreign residents to convert their licence into a Swiss licence within specified time limits. In the Canton of Basel-City, this procedure is managed by the Traffic Office (Amt für Verkehr), which supervises the theoretical and practical examinations necessary for homologation.
The conversion mainly depends on the country of origin of the licence. Those who come from a Member State of the European Union or the European Economic Area (EFTA) benefit from simplified procedures, thanks to the bilateral agreements and international treaties that Switzerland has signed. The exam is administered in Italian in the Canton of Ticino and in German in the Canton of Basel-City (or in French, depending on the official language of the canton). The test covers specific topics such as precedence, safety distances, behaviour in adverse weather conditions, load rules, speed limitations, and use of on-board technology.
The practical exam is a road test with an official observer assessing your driving skills in real-world settings. They check coordination, compliance with rules, perception of danger, and behavior in traffic. Both exams must be passed to obtain a Swiss licence.
The administrative procedure also includes a visual check and a review of the documentation. The Basel City Circulation Office requires that you apply with the following documents: passport or valid identity document, certificate of residence in Switzerland, original driver's license of the country of origin, medical certificate (if required according to age), and a photo card format compliant with Swiss standards.
